title: Basics: Working With Data in R
text:
This page covers the most practical basics you need before doing any statistics in R:

loading data
exploring structure
handling missing values
descriptive statistics
basic tables and proportions
random number generation
checking simple distribution shapes

You can use any dataset, but for this tutorial we work with:
perfectionism_total_scores.csv Small psychological teaching dataset containing one continuous variable: total maladaptive perfectionism score (FMPS_total). The data were adapted from the de-identified adult sample in Ferrari et al. (2018) and simplified for classroom use. In the original study, maladaptive perfectionism was computed as a combined score of four Frost Multidimensional Perfectionism Scale (FMPS) subscales: Concern over Mistakes, Parental Expectations, Parental Criticism, and Doubts about Actions.
Original study: Ferrari, M., Yap, K., Scott, N., Einstein, D. A., & Ciarrochi, J. (2018). Self-compassion moderates the perfectionism and depression link in both adolescence and adulthood. PLOS ONE, 13(2), e0192022. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0192022 ￼
Questionnaires used in the original study:

Frost Multidimensional Perfectionism Scale (FMPS) — 35 items. Used to derive maladaptive perfectionism (FMPS_total).
Self-Compassion Scale – Short Form (SCS-SF) — 12 items. Total self-compassion score (SELF_C).
Depression Anxiety Stress Scales – Short Form (DASS-21) — 21 items. Subscales for depression, anxiety, and stress.

Variables in our teaching file:

FMPS_total — total maladaptive perfectionism score (higher = more maladaptive perfectionism).
DASS_Depress — depression symptoms.
DASS_Anx — anxiety symptoms.
DASS_Stress — stress symptoms.
SELF_C — total self-compassion score.

Note: The teaching dataset keeps only variables needed for introductory analyses and may differ slightly in coding/format from the original supporting files.

 Download the dataset (perfectionism_total_scores.csv) 


library(kableExtra)
library(tidyverse)
df <- read_csv2("../assets/data/perfectionism_total_scores.csv")

title: Exploring the Apple Fitness Dataset
text:
This dataset contains 6,264 observations collected from an Apple Watch and Fitbit-like device.
Each row represents one time slice of recorded physical activity and biometric signals.
The variables describe:

demographic attributes (age, gender, height, weight)
physical activity metrics (steps, distance, calories)
heart-related measurements (hear_rate, resting_heart, entropy_heart, etc.)
computed features useful for modelling (corr_heart_steps, steps_times_distance)
the recorded activity class (activity), e.g. "Lying", "Sitting", "Walking", "Running"…

The dataset is ideal for demonstrating linear regression, feature engineering,
and exploratory visualisation because its variables are intuitive and quantitatively meaningful.

4. Basic structure of the dataset
The output of glimpse() shows 18 variables:

age, gender, height, weight
steps, hear_rate, distance, calories
entropy_heart, entropy_setps
resting_heart, norm_heart, sd_norm_heart

We will use these variables to introduce linear regression step by step — from simple models to more advanced ones (interactions, multivariate regression, transformations, diagnostics, etc.).

title: Exploring the Apple Fitness Dataset
section: Packages for regression in this chapter
text:
Packages for regression in this chapter
In this chapter we will work with a small, focused toolbox for regression models in R.

Base stats (lm() function) Simple linear and multiple regression using base R. We use it as the core engine: lm(hear_rate ~ steps, data = apple) is our starting point for modelling.
broom Tidies model output into tibbles.

tidy() – coefficients in a neat table,
augment() – fitted values and residuals attached to the original data,
glance() – one-row summary (R², AIC, …). This makes regression results easy to combine with dplyr and ggplot2.

Optional: modelr Helper functions like add_predictions() and add_residuals(). We will mostly rely on broom, but you may encounter modelr in other tutorials.
Optional: tidymodels A modern modelling framework with a unified grammar for regression, classification, resampling, and tuning. We briefly show how linear_reg() with engine "lm" reproduces the basic lm() workflow, and how the same interface extends to more complex models.
Optional: diagnostics packages (performance, car) For this R-focused course we keep diagnostics simple (plots and a few summary numbers). For deeper regression diagnostics (multicollinearity, detailed ANOVA, assumption checks), packages like performance or car are good next steps, especially in a statistics-oriented course.

title: Exploring the Apple Fitness Dataset
text:
6. First simple model: calories ~ steps
A natural first question:
How strongly are burned calories related to the number of steps?
We start with a simple linear regression:

model_simple <- lm(calories ~ steps, data = apple)
model_simple


Call:
lm(formula = calories ~ steps, data = apple)

Coefficients:
(Intercept)        steps  
   22.84232     -0.03076  


The printed output shows the intercept and slope, but is not very tidy. We can use broom::tidy() instead:

tidy(model_simple)

# A tibble: 2 × 5
  term        estimate std.error statistic  p.value
  <chr>          <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>
1 (Intercept)  22.8      0.372        61.4 0       
2 steps        -0.0308   0.00150     -20.5 1.37e-90



the intercept is the expected calories when steps = 0,
the slope tells us how many calories increase on average when we add one step.

(Because steps can be large, it may be more interpretable to rescale them, for example to thousands of steps, later in the chapter.)

6.1 Visualising the simple regression line

apple %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = steps, y = calories)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, color = "#619CFF") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "#F8766D") +
  labs(
    title = "Simple linear regression: calories ~ steps",
    x = "Steps",
    y = "Calories"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)








The regression line shows the average trend; the scatter of points around the line represents unexplained variability.
⸻

8. Basic diagnostics for the simple model

8.1 Residuals vs fitted values

apple_aug %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = .fitted, y = .resid)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey50") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, color = "#619CFF") +
  labs(
    title = "Residuals vs fitted values",
    x = "Fitted calories",
    y = "Residuals"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)








We would like to see: * roughly constant spread of residuals across the range of fitted values, * no strong curvature.


8.2 Histogram and Q–Q plot of residuals

# Histogram
apple_aug %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = .resid)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "#619CFF", color = "white") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of residuals",
    x = "Residual",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)







# Q-Q plot
apple_aug %>%
  ggplot(aes(sample = .resid)) +
  stat_qq(color = "#619CFF") +
  stat_qq_line(color = "#F8766D") +
  labs(

    x = "Theoretical quantiles",

Interpretation reminder
For this course we keep diagnostics informal and visual. In a full statistics course, you would add formal tests (normality, homoscedasticity) and check for influential points.

10. Visualising model predictions
To keep the plot in two dimensions, we can fix some variables and vary only one of them. For example, fix hear_rate at its median and see how predicted calories grow with steps.

hear_median <- median(apple$hear_rate, na.rm = TRUE)

pred_grid <- tibble(
  steps     = seq(min(apple$steps), max(apple$steps), length.out = 100),
  distance  = median(apple$distance, na.rm = TRUE),
  hear_rate = hear_median
)

pred_grid <- pred_grid %>%
  mutate(calories_pred = predict(model_multi, newdata = pred_grid))

ggplot() +
  geom_point(
    data = apple,
    aes(x = steps, y = calories),
    alpha = 0.2,
    color = "#B3CDE3"
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = pred_grid,
    aes(x = steps, y = calories_pred),
    color = "#F8766D",
    linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Predicted calories as a function of steps",
    subtitle = "Distance and heart rate fixed at their medians",
    x = "Steps",
    y = "Calories"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)








This connects the algebraic model to a visual, more intuitive understanding.

text:
11. Optional: interaction term
You might suspect that the effect of steps is different for low vs high heart rate. This can be expressed by an interaction:
model_interaction <- lm(calories ~ steps * hear_rate + distance, data = apple) tidy(model_interaction)
The term steps:hear_rate captures how the slope of steps changes with heart rate.






Tip



When to use interactions?
Use interaction terms when: * you expect the effect of one predictor to depend on the level of another predictor, * and you can explain such dependence substantively (not only because a p-value is small).

2. Flipping a coin with rbinom()
rbinom() generates random outcomes from a binomial distribution: • n = number of generated observations • size = number of trials (e.g. number of flips) • prob = probability of success on each trial

2.1 One coin, one flip

2.2 One coin, many flips

[1] 0.0009765625




8.2 Cumulative probabilities with pbinom()

[1] 0.3769531

8.3 Theoretical mean and variance
For X (n, p):

(X) = np
(X) = np(1 - p)


size <- 100  # number of coins
prob <- 0.5  # probability of heads

data.frame(
    var  = round(size * prob * (1 - prob), 3),
    sd   = round(sqrt(size * prob * (1 - prob)), 3),
    mean = size * prob
)

title: Binomial distribution: coin flips
text:
9. Example: “Extreme” result with 100 coins

9.1 Example: How extreme is 56 heads out of 100?
We now switch from intuition (simulation) to exact probability using the binomial distribution (X (100, 0.5)\).
The expected number of heads is:

mean = 50
standard deviation = \(\sqrt{100 \cdot 0.5 \cdot 0.5} = 5\)

So 56 heads is more than 1 SD above the mean, and values of 44 or fewer are symmetric on the left.
This motivates the idea of a two-tailed test: “How surprising is it to be this far from the mean (on either side)?”

dbinom(x = 56, size = 100, prob = 0.5)

[1] 0.03895256


The value 0.03895 means that if the coin is truly fair, the probability of getting exactly 56 heads out of 100 flips is about 3.9%.
In other words, if you repeated this experiment many times (always 100 flips of a fair coin), you would expect an outcome of exactly 56 heads in roughly 4 out of 100 experiments. It’s rare, but not impossible — which is exactly the kind of “unusual but still plausible” event that hypothesis tests are built around.


9.2 Two-tailed probability: 56 or more heads, OR 44 or fewer
We look at:

right tail: 56, 57, …, 100
left tail: 0, 1, …, 44 (because 50 – (56 – 50) = 44)

We now compute the probability of being at least this extreme in both tails:

n <- 100
p <- 0.5

# P(X >= 56)

P_ge_56 <- sum(dbinom(x = 56:100, size = n, prob = p))

# P(X <= 44)

P_le_44 <- sum(dbinom(x = 0:44, size = n, prob = p))

# Two-tailed probability

P_ge_56 + P_le_44

[1] 0.271253








Interpreting the two-tailed probability



The value of 0.27 means that about 27 % of all outcomes (under a perfectly fair coin) are at least as extreme as getting 56 heads out of 100 tosses.

What does “as extreme” mean?
We consider outcomes that are at least 6 away from the mean (50):

Right tail: 56, 57, …, 100
Left tail: 44, 43, …, 0 (because 56 is 6 above the mean → we also check 6 below the mean)

This includes many results, not just a single number — which is why the probability is much larger than P(X = 56).


Why is 27 % not surprising?
Because in a two-tailed test we ask:

“How often would we see a result at least this far from the mean if the coin were fair?”

The answer is: 👉 Roughly one out of four experiments will produce a result this extreme or more.
So 56 heads out of 100 is perfectly compatible with a fair coin. It is not evidence of bias.





9.3 Visualising the extremeness

# Compute the full binomial distribution
df <- data.frame(
  heads = 0:100,
  prob  = dbinom(0:100, size = 100, prob = 0.5)
)

df <- df %>%
  mutate(
    extreme = (heads >= 56) | (heads <= 44)   # highlight tail areas
  )

ggplot(df, aes(x = heads, y = prob, fill = extreme)) +
    geom_col() +
    scale_fill_manual(
        values = c("FALSE" = "grey80", "TRUE" = "#FC4E07"),
        labels = c("Typical outcomes", "Extreme outcomes")
    ) +
    labs(
        title = "Two-tailed extremeness for 100 coin flips",
        subtitle = "Values ≥ 56 or ≤ 44 are symmetric deviations from the mean (50)",
        x = "Number of heads",
        y = "Exact probability P(X = x)"
    ) +
        theme_minimal(base_size = 16) +
        theme(
        legend.title = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "bottom"
    )










9.4 Interpretation






How to read this graph (interpretation)



This visualisation shows exact probabilities for all possible numbers of heads in 100 coin flips.

What the shape tells us

The center (around 50) holds most of the probability mass. This is what you expect from a fair coin: outcomes cluster tightly around the mean.
The orange bars highlight the extreme regions:

56, 57, …, 100 on the right
44, 43, …, 0 on the left These values are equally “far from the mean” in either direction.

Each orange bar individually is rare, and together they form the total probability of “being at least this far from 50”.



What this means for our example
A result like 56 heads is surprising — but not shocking. About 27 % of all experiments would produce an outcome at least this extreme (either ≥ 56 or ≤ 44), even if the coin is perfectly fair.
In other words:

Unusual outcomes happen quite often. A single result like 56/100 is not strong evidence that the coin is biased.



Connection to hypothesis testing
This is exactly the logic behind two-sided p-values: we evaluate how often we would observe a result at least this extreme under the assumption that nothing unusual is happening.

title: 3D regression surface with plotly
text:
Step 2 — Understanding the SVR model
In this step we train a Support Vector Regression (SVR) model to learn the relationship:
\[
\text{Petal.Width} = f(\text{Sepal.Width},\ \text{Sepal.Length})
\]
The goal is not classification, but a smooth, flexible regression surface that later becomes the 3D plot.


Support Vector Regression (SVR) in simple terms
SVR is designed to capture non-linear patterns while keeping the fitted function smooth and controlled. It does this by:

allowing small errors (inside an ε-tube)
penalising larger errors
using a kernel function (here: RBF) to bend the surface in non-linear ways

The result is a balanced, smooth 3D surface that follows the structure of the data without overfitting.



Key parts of the printed model output

SV type: eps-svr (regression)
This is a regression-oriented variant of SVM. Instead of predicting classes, it predicts a continuous outcome (Petal.Width).


epsilon = 0.1
Epsilon defines the width of the “tube” within which errors are ignored.

larger ε → smoother surface
smaller ε → more detailed, potentially wiggly fit



cost C = 1
C controls how strongly the model penalizes errors outside the ε-tube.

high C → the model tries to fit almost everything
low C → more regularized, more stable surface

Here, C = 1 gives a well-balanced, conservative model.


Gaussian RBF kernel
The radial-basis kernel allows the model to bend and warp the fitted surface. Without it (e.g., using a linear kernel), the result would be almost a flat plane.
RBF produces the smooth hills and valleys you later see in the 3D plot.


sigma
Sigma determines how wide the influence of each point is:

small sigma → very wiggly surface
large sigma → very smooth surface

Sigma is estimated automatically from the data.


Number of support vectors
Support vectors are the points that lie outside the ε-tube. These are the data points that actually shape the regression surface.
In this example: 116 support vectors out of 150 flowers → the data have quite a bit of non-linear structure.


Training error
Indicates how closely the model matches the training data. A value around 0.12 means the average error is about 0.12 cm of Petal.Width — very reasonable.




Summary
This step fits a non-linear SVR model that can describe how Sepal.Width and Sepal.Length jointly predict Petal.Width. The RBF kernel gives the model flexibility, while parameters like ε and C keep the surface stable and smooth. The trained model is then used in the next steps to generate predictions on a grid and to construct the interactive 3D surface.

model <- svm_rbf(cost = 1.0) %>%
  set_engine("kernlab") %>%
  set_mode("regression") %>%
  fit(Petal.Width ~ Sepal.Width + Sepal.Length, data = iris)

Step 3 — Creating the prediction grid
To draw a smooth 3D surface, the model needs to be evaluated not only on the observed data points, but on a dense grid that covers the entire Sepal.Width × Sepal.Length space.
We therefore:

compute the minimum and maximum of both predictors
generate sequences (xrange, yrange) with a small step (mesh_size = 0.02)
combine them into a 2D lattice using meshgrid()

This grid contains thousands of (x, y) points, evenly spaced across the whole plane. These points will later receive predicted Petal.Width values, forming the smooth surface.
The grid itself has no biology in it — it is simply a mathematical canvas on which we paint the regression model.

x_max <- max(X$Sepal.Width) - margin
y_min <- min(X$Sepal.Length) - margin
y_max <- max(X$Sepal.Length) - margin

Step 4 — Predicting values on the grid
The SVR model was trained on the real iris flowers, but here we need predictions for every point in the artificial grid.
We therefore:

reshape the grid matrices (xx, yy) into long column vectors
combine them into a two-column matrix (final)
feed all points into the trained model at once
reshape the predictions back into a matrix with the same dimensions as the grid

This gives us a predicted Petal.Width value for every location in the grid, turning the learned SVR function into a smooth 3D surface.
The result (pred) is a matrix perfectly aligned with the grid and ready to be plotted using plotly’s add_surface().

title: 3D regression surface with plotly
text:
Interacting with the 3D plot
The plotly figure is not just a static picture – you can explore the fitted surface interactively:

Rotate – click and drag with the left mouse button to change the viewing angle.
Zoom – use the mouse wheel or the Zoom tool in the toolbar to move closer or farther away.
Pan – drag with the right mouse button (or with a two-finger drag on a trackpad) to shift the whole scene.
Reset view – double-click inside the plot or click the home icon in the toolbar to go back to the default view.
Hover tooltips – move the mouse over points to see the exact Sepal.Width, Sepal.Length, and Petal.Width values.
Toggle traces – if the plot contains multiple layers, clicking entries in the legend turns individual traces on and off.
Download as image – the camera icon saves the current view as a PNG file. (This works most reliably in a web browser; in some embedded viewers it may be limited.)

Some toolbar icons are shared between 2D and 3D plots, so a few tools may appear less useful here (for example, 2D lasso selection on a 3D surface). For this example, rotation, zooming, panning and hover tooltips are the most important interactions.

title: Gapminder Bubble Animation with Plotly
section: Did you notice anything interesting in 1992?
text:
Did you notice anything interesting in 1992?
Have a look at the animation — does anything look unusual?







Explanation





The dramatic collapse around 1992–1994 in Rwanda, Africa is real data — not an artefact.
It reflects the Rwandan genocide (1994) and the preceding civil war. In the span of a few months, roughly 800,000 people were killed, the health system collapsed, and mortality skyrocketed.
Gapminder uses 5-year intervals (1987 → 1992 → 1997), so the destruction of 1994 appears as a sharp fall in the 1992 data point.
This is one of the clearest examples where historical events leave a visible fingerprint in demographic data.
You can also tell that Rwanda is not the only country with a story hidden in the dots:

Several southern African countries (e.g., Botswana, Zimbabwe, South Africa) show a fall in life expectancy in the 1990s associated with the HIV/AIDS epidemic.
Some post-Soviet countries show stagnation or even decreases in life expectancy and income after the collapse of the USSR.
Other countries (for example in East Asia) show long, smooth climbs in income and life expectancy that correspond to periods of rapid economic development.

title: Gapminder Bubble Animation with Plotly
section: Are GDP per capita and life expectancy related?
text:
Are GDP per capita and life expectancy related?







Explanation





The overall Pearson correlation in the full Gapminder dataset is r ≈ 0.58 (p < .001), with a confidence interval roughly 0.55–0.61.

cor.test(gapminder$lifeExp, gapminder$gdpPercap)


    Pearson's product-moment correlation

data:  gapminder$lifeExp and gapminder$gdpPercap
t = 29.658, df = 1702, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.5515065 0.6141690
sample estimates:
      cor 
0.5837062 

ggplot(gapminder, aes(x = lifeExp, y = gdpPercap)) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
    facet_wrap(~continent) +
    theme_light()








This means:

Countries with higher income per person tend to have longer life expectancy.
The relationship is strong, but not perfect – several regions rise faster or slower depending on history, politics, healthcare, or conflict.
In the animation, this appears as a general upward-right trend: bubbles move toward higher GDP and higher life expectancy over time.

Interpreting this correlation requires some care:

GDP per capita does not biologically “cause” longer life.
Instead, it serves as a proxy for infrastructure, stability, healthcare availability, sanitation, education, and reduced child mortality, all of which increase average lifespan.
Large deviations (e.g., sudden drops in Rwanda or HIV-related declines in southern Africa) reveal how historical shocks can break this pattern.

So while r ≈ 0.58 might look like a simple number, in context it summarises decades of global public-health, economics, and political history.




Bonus task – per-continent correlation
Can you compute the correlation between GDP per capita and life expectancy separately for each continent?
Hint: Instead of writing five separate cor.test() calls, try to use a grouped workflow and let R repeat the test for you.







Suggested solution





One neat approach is to combine:

group_by(continent) – to split the data into continent-wise groups
nest() – to store each group’s rows in a list-column data
map() – to run cor.test() on each nested dataset
broom::tidy() – to turn the test output into a clean tibble

library(tidyverse)

gapminder %>%
  group_by(continent) %>%
  nest() %>%
  mutate(
    cor_test = map(
      data,
      ~ cor.test(.x$lifeExp, .x$gdpPercap, use = "complete.obs")
    ),
    tidy_cor = map(cor_test, broom::tidy)
  ) %>%
  select(continent, tidy_cor) %>%
  unnest(tidy_cor)

title: Tufte’s principles (and how to avoid lying with axes)
text:
This page is a small, visual reminder of a few ideas from Edward Tufte:
We’ll illustrate that with a simple example from the gapminder dataset.
library(tidyverse)
library(gapminder)

title: Tufte’s principles (and how to avoid lying with axes)
section: Example: life expectancy in Peru before 1980
text:
Example: life expectancy in Peru before 1980

life_exp_pre80 <- gapminder %>%
  filter(country == "Peru", year < 1980)


1) A misleading plot (truncated y‑axis)
This plot zooms the y‑axis to a narrow range.
It makes the improvement in life expectancy look much larger than it really is.

life_exp_pre80 %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = lifeExp, fill = as.factor(year))) +
  geom_col() +
  theme_light() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(43.9, 60)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 43.9, color = "red", size = 2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 58.45, color = "red", size = 2) +
  geom_label(
    aes(x = 1960, y = 58.45, fill = NULL),
    label = "Ratio is about 4.5",
    size = 10
  )










2) The honest version (axis starts at zero)
Same data, same geom, same colors.
Only the axis range is fixed so the magnitude is not exaggerated.

life_exp_pre80 %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = lifeExp, fill = as.factor(year))) +
  geom_col() +
  theme_light() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 60)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 43.9, color = "red", size = 2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 58.45, color = "red", size = 2) +
  geom_label(
    aes(x = 1960, y = 58.45, fill = NULL),
    label = "Ratio is about 1.3",
    size = 10
  )










Quick check (the real ratio)

max_life_exp <- life_exp_pre80 %>% slice_max(lifeExp)
min_life_exp <- life_exp_pre80 %>% slice_min(lifeExp)

max_life_exp$lifeExp / min_life_exp$lifeExp

[1] 1.331306




3) A deliberately “bad” example (what not to do)
This plot is purposely overloaded. It demonstrates the classic mistakes that Tufte warns about: too much background, heavy gridlines, loud colors, and no clear message.
Goal: Help students see how easily a plot can become cluttered.

gapminder %>%
    filter(country == "Peru", year < 1980) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = year, y = lifeExp, fill = as.factor(year))) +
        geom_col() +
        theme(
            panel.grid.major = element_line(size = 1, linetype = 'dashed', colour = "green"),
            panel.grid.minor = element_line(size = 1, linetype = 'dashed', colour = "blue"),
            panel.background = element_rect(fill = "red", colour = "blue"),
            plot.background = element_rect(fill = "green")
        )










4) A cleaned-up reference version
Same data, but now the plot is readable. The layout is simple, the background is neutral, and unnecessary visual elements are removed.
Goal: Show the transition from visual noise to a reasonable starting point.

gapminder %>%
    filter(country == "Peru", year < 1980) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = year, y = lifeExp, fill = as.factor(year))) +
        geom_col() +
        theme_light() +
        theme(legend.position = "none")










5) Highlighting one meaningful value (Tufte-ish)
Here we finally work with visual hierarchy: one bar (1967) is emphasized while everything else fades into the background. No gridlines, minimal text, and clear focus on the information that matters.
Goal: Demonstrate that a minimalist plot can be far more informative than a decorative one.

gapminder %>%
    filter(country == "Peru", year < 1980) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = year, y = lifeExp, fill = (year == 1967))) +
        geom_col() +
        theme_minimal() +
        theme(
            axis.text.y = element_blank(),
            legend.position = "none") +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("gray", "red")) +
    geom_text(
    aes(x = year, y = lifeExp, label = round(lifeExp)), nudge_y = 0.25, size = 7, vjust = 2, color = "black")

title: Tufte’s principles (and how to avoid lying with axes)
text:
Take-home message

If your axis does not start at zero, explain why and check that it does not distort the story.
Prefer clarity over decoration.
The “best” theme is the one that makes the data the easiest to read.
Highlight only what carries meaning. Silence around the important signal helps it stand out.

title: Correlation in R
text:
This page walks through several ways of working with correlations in R, using two small teaching datasets:
The goal is not only to compute a single cor() value, but to learn how to:

title: Correlation in R
text:
Setup

library(tidyverse)


# install.packages("corrplot")
# install.packages("lares")
library(corrplot)
library(lares)

# Load datasets
# Adjust paths to match your project structure
icecream <- read_csv("../assets/data/ice_cream.csv")
crime    <- read_csv("../assets/data/crime.csv")

title: Correlation in R
text:
1. Ice-cream experiment: basic correlations
In this dataset, participants completed:

a puzzle task (puzzle), and

a video game task (video).

We start with the simplest question:

How strongly are puzzle scores and video game scores related?


1.1 Pearson correlation

cor(icecream$puzzle, icecream$video)

[1] 0.465106


You can also use the formula interface with with():

with(icecream, cor(puzzle, video))

[1] 0.465106




1.2 Visualising the relationship
Base R plot version (quick and simple):

plot(
  icecream$puzzle, icecream$video,
  main = "Correlation between puzzle score\nand video game score",
  xlab = "Puzzle score",
  ylab = "Video game score",
  sub  = paste0("r = ", round(cor(icecream$puzzle, icecream$video), 2))
)









Bonus task: Recreate this plot using ggplot2 instead of base R.



1.3 Non-parametric correlations
Sometimes variables are not normally distributed or contain outliers. Two common rank-based alternatives are:

Spearman’s rho
Kendall’s tau


# Spearman's rank correlation
cor(icecream$puzzle, icecream$video, method = "spearman")

[1] 0.4807849

# Kendall's tau
cor(icecream$puzzle, icecream$video, method = "kendall")

[1] 0.3657759



Reflection prompt:
Compare the Pearson, Spearman, and Kendall coefficients.
Are they similar, or do ranks tell a different story?

section: 2. Crime data: correlation matrices and tests
text:
2. Crime data: correlation matrices and tests
The crime dataset contains several numeric variables such as:

CrimeRate – crime per population

Males – number of males in the labour force

Wage – average wage

StateSize – size of the state, and many others.


2.1 Simple correlation matrix
We can compute a correlation matrix for a small subset of variables:

crime %>%
  select(CrimeRate, Males, Wage) %>%
  cor()

CrimeRate 1.0000000 0.1571129 0.4248530
Males     0.1571129 1.0000000 0.1796086

CrimeRate      1.00  0.16 0.42
Males          0.16  1.00 0.18
Wage           0.42  0.18 1.00

A quick way to visualise all pairwise relationships is pairs():

crime %>%
  select(CrimeRate, Males, Wage) %>%
  pairs()









Bonus task: Which pairs look most linear and which look weak or non-linear?



2.3 Testing correlations: cor.test()
cor() only gives you the coefficient.
Use cor.test() when you want a hypothesis test and a confidence interval.

# Test correlation between Males and Wage
cor.test(crime$Males, crime$Wage)

text:
3. Correlations by group
Sometimes you do not just want “one correlation for everybody”, but separate correlations within subgroups.
In the crime data, variable MoreMales indicates whether the state has a particularly high number of males.

3.1 Grouped correlation (summarise version)
Here we compute the correlation between StateSize and Education separately for each value of MoreMales:

crime %>%
  select(CrimeRate, StateSize, Education, Wage, MoreMales) %>%
  group_by(MoreMales) %>%
  summarise(
    cor_StateSize_Education = cor(StateSize, Education, use = "complete.obs")
  )

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  MoreMales cor_StateSize_Education
      <dbl>                   <dbl>
1         0                  0.0210
2         1                  0.0135


This approach is:

readable,

uses only dplyr,

easy to adapt to other variable pairs.



3.2 Grouped correlation (nested + purrr version)
The same idea, but written in a more functional style:

library(purrr)
library(broom)

crime %>%
  select(CrimeRate, StateSize, Education, Wage, MoreMales) %>%
  group_by(MoreMales) %>%
  nest() %>%
  mutate(
    cor_test = map(
      data,
      ~ cor.test(.x$StateSize, .x$Education, use = "complete.obs")
    ),
    tidy_result = map(cor_test, broom::tidy)
  ) %>%
  select(MoreMales, tidy_result) %>%
  unnest(tidy_result)

# A tibble: 2 × 9
# Groups:   MoreMales [2]
  MoreMales estimate statistic p.value parameter conf.low conf.high method      
      <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>     <int>    <dbl>     <dbl> <chr>       
1         0   0.0210    0.126    0.900        36   -0.301     0.338 Pearson's p…
2         1   0.0135    0.0357   0.973         7   -0.657     0.672 Pearson's p…

nest() creates a small tibble for each group in column data.

map_dbl() applies cor() inside each small dataset.


This pattern is a gentle introduction to the “split–apply–combine” idea using nested data frames.

title: Correlation in R
section: 4. Visualising correlations in larger sets of variables
text:
4. Visualising correlations in larger sets of variables

4.1 Correlation heatmap with corrplot
For many variables, a correlation matrix is easier to read as a heatmap.
The next block:

Keeps only numeric variables.
Drops variables with missing values or zero variance.
Randomly picks 10 numeric variables (just for demo).
Computes a correlation matrix.
Plots it with corrplot() and hierarchical clustering.


set.seed(123)  # for reproducible sampling of columns

crime %>%
  select_if(is.numeric) %>%               # keep only numeric variables
  select_if(~ !any(is.na(.))) %>%        # drop variables with any missing values
  select_if(~ sd(.) != 0) %>%            # drop variables with zero variance
  select(sample(names(.), size = 10)) %>%
  cor(use = "complete.obs") %>%          # row-wise removal of missing values
  corrplot::corrplot(order = "hclust")   # cluster similar variables









Bonus task: Choose your own subset of variables and interpret at least three interesting pairs.
